executiveSummary: The planet has warmed about 1.3°C since pre-industrial times, driven by fossil-fuel CO2. The impacts are already measurable and costly, but clean energy is now the cheapest option for most of the world. The gap between pledges and the 1.5°C path is where our choices matter.

slides.subtitle: What the data says, what it costs, and what is working
slides.visualDescription: Satellite view of Earth at night with glowing city lights and a thin blue atmosphere
slides.speakerNotes: Thanks for making time. This is a 25-minute tour of the evidence, the stakes, and the response.

keyBullets: The signal: what we measure
The cause: where emissions come from
The stakes: impacts already here
The response: what is working
What we can do
slides.speakerNotes: Five parts. I'll keep the numbers tight and leave time for questions.

slides.subtitle: What the instruments tell us
slides.visualDescription: Weather balloon rising over Antarctic ice
slides.speakerNotes: Start with measurement, not models.

slides.slideTitle: 2024 Was the Hottest Year on Record
slides.subtitle: Global average temperature above the 1850–1900 baseline
keyBullets: 1.55°C: above pre-industrial, the first calendar year past 1.5°C
Each of the last ten years ranks among the ten warmest
slides.visualDescription: Heat map of the globe in deep reds
slides.speakerNotes: WMO consolidated six datasets. One year above 1.5 is not the Paris breach, which is a 20-year average, but it is a warning.
slides.supportingFacts: WMO State of the Global Climate 2024

slides.subtitle: Global temperature anomaly, °C vs 1850–1900
keyBullets: Warming since 1980 runs at about 0.2°C per decade
slides.speakerNotes: Flat for a century, then a steady climb. The slope is the story.

slides.slideTitle: CO2 Is Higher Than at Any Time in 800,000 Years
slides.subtitle: Atmospheric CO2, parts per million
keyBullets: From 280 ppm before industry to 424 ppm in 2024
slides.speakerNotes: Ice cores give us 800,000 years of record; the range was 180 to 300. We are at 424.

slides.slideTitle: Every Vital Sign Points the Same Way
keyBullets: 4.5 mm/yr: sea level rise, double the 1990s rate
−13%: Arctic summer ice per decade
270 Gt: ice Greenland loses each year
90%: of the excess heat absorbed by the ocean
slides.speakerNotes: Independent instruments, independent teams, one direction.

slides.subtitle: Where the emissions come from
slides.speakerNotes: Now the why.

slides.subtitle: Share of global greenhouse gas emissions by sector
keyBullets: Power, transport, buildings, and industry together make up 73%
slides.speakerNotes: Agriculture and land use are real, but energy is the lever.

keyBullets: Historical: the US and Europe emitted nearly half of all CO2 since 1850
Today: China emits about 31%, the US 13%, India 8%, the EU 7%
slides.speakerNotes: Responsibility and leverage are different maps.

slides.slideTitle: We Are on a Highway to Climate Hell
keyBullets: "We are on a highway to climate hell with our foot still on the accelerator."
António Guterres, UN Secretary-General, COP27, 2022
slides.speakerNotes: Strong words from a careful diplomat.

slides.subtitle: Impacts already here
slides.speakerNotes: This is not a future problem.

slides.subtitle: 1.5°C versus 2°C of warming
keyBullets: 1.5°C versus 2°C
Extreme heat: 14% of people exposed every five years, versus 37%
Coral reefs: 70–90% lost, versus more than 99%
Arctic ice-free summers: once a century, versus once a decade
slides.speakerNotes: IPCC SR1.5. Every tenth of a degree is measured in lives and ecosystems.

keyBullets: 2021: Pacific Northwest heat dome, 49.6°C in Canada
2022: Pakistan floods, a third of the country under water
2023: Canada's wildfires burn 18 million hectares
2024: Hottest year on record, 1.55°C
slides.speakerNotes: Each of these was called unprecedented. Then the next one came.

slides.slideTitle: 3.5 Billion People Live in Highly Vulnerable Places
keyBullets: 3.5B: people in contexts highly vulnerable to climate change
Nearly half of humanity, per the IPCC's 2022 assessment
slides.visualDescription: Aerial photo of a flooded village
slides.speakerNotes: IPCC AR6 WGII. This is where adaptation money has to go.

slides.subtitle: What is working
slides.visualDescription: Wind turbines over the sea at sunrise
slides.speakerNotes: Now the turn.

slides.slideTitle: Solar Power Got 90% Cheaper in a Decade
slides.subtitle: Utility-scale solar, levelized cost, $/MWh
keyBullets: Solar is now the cheapest electricity in history
slides.speakerNotes: IRENA. The economics have flipped.

slides.slideTitle: 30% of the World's Electricity Is Now Renewable
keyBullets: 30%: of global electricity from renewables in 2023
Up from 19% in 2000, driven by solar and wind
slides.speakerNotes: Ember Global Electricity Review 2024.

slides.slideTitle: Clean Energy Investment Now Doubles Fossil
slides.subtitle: Global energy investment in 2024, trillions of dollars
keyBullets: $2 trillion went to clean energy, against $1.1 trillion to fossil fuels
slides.speakerNotes: IEA World Energy Investment 2024.

keyBullets: Clean the grid: triple renewables by 2030
Electrify: vehicles, heat pumps, industrial heat
Cut methane: 75% from fossil fuel operations
Remove the rest: forests, soils, and direct capture
slides.speakerNotes: IEA's net-zero roadmap in four moves.

keyBullets: Current policies: about 2.7°C of warming by 2100
Paris-aligned path: 1.5°C, with emissions halved by 2030
slides.speakerNotes: Climate Action Tracker. The gap is the work.

slides.subtitle: In our work and our lives
slides.speakerNotes: Bring it home.

keyBullets: Measure: baseline our travel and cloud emissions this quarter
Choose: default to rail and video where they work
Buy: green tariffs for our offices
Share: report progress at each all-hands
slides.speakerNotes: Four concrete moves we can own.

keyBullets: What surprised you most?
Where can our team move fastest?
slides.speakerNotes: Open the floor.

slides.subtitle: Thank you
keyBullets: The tools exist and they are cheap; the choice is ours
